description_full: Chemed Corporation provides hospice and palliative care services to patients through a network of physicians, doctors, registered nurses, home health aides, social workers, clergy, and volunteers primarily in the United States. The company operates through two segments: VITAS and Roto-Rooter segments. The company offers plumbing, drain cleaning, excavation, water restoration, and other related services to residential and commercial customers through company-owned branches, independent contractors, and franchisees. The company also provides direct medical services to patients, as well as spiritual and emotional counseling to both patients and their families. Chemed Corporation was incorporated in 1970 and is headquartered in Cincinnati, Ohio.
ceo_bio: Mr. Kevin J. McNamara | CEO, President & Director | Age 71 | Compensation: $4.9M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 15K people. Revenue per employee of $160K ranks in the bottom quartile among Healthcare peers. Each employee generates $21K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 31× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: Chemed Corp is a mid-cap healthcare business with a $7.1B market cap on $2.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 32% against a 8% cost of capital — a 24-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $325M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 6.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 13% over the past year excluding the latest month.

val: The stock trades 15% below its DCF fair value of $646, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 60%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $510 to $848 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 12% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.5% (vs the 8% bar).

The price implies 4.8% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 32% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 24pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.46x.
ROE of 27% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Goodwill makes up 43% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.8% over 3 years, 4.0% over 5 years and 5.1% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 2.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 2.7% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (8 sales, net $6.8M sold).
It returns 6.5% a year to shareholders (6.1% in buybacks and 0.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 37 consecutive years, raising it 8.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 15,811 employees, each generates about $160K of revenue, 0.4x the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 4.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $21K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.9M (31x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
